history.heading: Caquetío and Spanish era
paragraphs: Aruba, a small arid island off the coast of Venezuela, was inhabited by the Caquetío people, an Arawak group from the mainland, whose rock paintings can still be seen in caves. The Spanish claimed the island in 1499 but considered it useless for plantations and deported much of the population to work in Hispaniola.
The Dutch took control in 1636 during their war with Spain, and Aruba was governed for long periods as part of the Dutch colony of Curaçao, used mainly for livestock grazing.

history.heading: Gold, oil and autonomy
paragraphs: A gold rush in the 19th century brought some prosperity, followed by aloe cultivation. In 1924 a large oil refinery opened at San Nicolas, attracting workers from across the Caribbean and transforming the island's economy and population.

Aruba was part of the Netherlands Antilles from 1954, but a strong movement for separate status, led by Betico Croes, achieved results: on 1 January 1986 Aruba became a separate constituent country within the Kingdom of the Netherlands.

culture.heading: Language and festivals
paragraphs: Papiamento, a Creole language mixing Portuguese, Spanish, Dutch and African languages, is spoken by most Arubans and is official alongside Dutch. Many people also speak English and Spanish.

Carnival is the biggest celebration, with weeks of parades, music and costumes. Local dishes include keshi yena (stuffed cheese), pastechi and fresh fish. The island's national anthem and flag date from 1976.

politics.heading: Constituent country
paragraphs: Aruba is one of four countries in the Kingdom of the Netherlands, together with the Netherlands, Curaçao and Sint Maarten. The Dutch monarch is head of state, represented by a governor. Aruba runs its internal affairs through an elected parliament (Staten) and a prime minister, while the kingdom handles defence and foreign policy.
Aruba is not part of the European Union, but Arubans hold Dutch citizenship.

economy.heading: Tourism
paragraphs: Tourism is by far the largest industry, with visitors drawn by white beaches, constant sunshine and its location outside the hurricane belt. Most tourists come from the United States.

The oil refinery, once the economic backbone, closed and has operated only intermittently since 2009. The currency is the Aruban florin, pegged to the US dollar. Aruba has one of the highest living standards in the Caribbean.
